summary.text: Writing \(B_{n-1}=N/D\) in lowest terms, the proof first shows that the relevant rational is integral exactly when \(n^2\mid Nn+D\).  Faulhaber’s formula and the von Staudt–Clausen valuation rule—an odd prime \(p\) occurs exactly once in \(D\) precisely when \(p-1\mid n-1\)—then establish prime-power by prime-power that this divisibility is equivalent to \(n\mid \sum_{k=0}^{n-1}k^{n-1}+1\), with even \(n\) handled separately; the two conjectures therefore have the same pointwise condition.

full_proof.text:
Let \(B_m\) denote the standard Bernoulli numbers, with \(B_1=-\tfrac12\). Write every Bernoulli number in lowest terms as
\[
 B_m=\frac{N_m}{D_m},\qquad N_m\in\mathbb Z,\quad D_m\in\mathbb N_{>0},\quad \gcd(|N_m|,D_m)=1.
\]
Thus, if \(B_m=0\), then \(N_m=0\) and \(D_m=1\).

For \(n>1\), put \(m=n-1\), and abbreviate
\[
 N=N_m,\qquad D=D_m,
 \qquad S=S_m(n):=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}k^m.
\]
We shall prove the pointwise equivalence
\[
 a(n)=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad n\mid S+1. \tag{1}
\]
Since the right side is precisely the Agoh–Giuga congruence for \(n>1\), this pointwise equivalence will immediately imply the equivalence of the two conjectures.

We first establish the Bernoulli-denominator facts and power-sum facts needed in the proof.

## 1. Power sums modulo a prime

Let \(p\) be a prime and let \(r\ge 1\). In the finite field \(\mathbb F_p\),
\[
 \sum_{x\in\mathbb F_p}x^r=
 \begin{cases}
 -1,&p-1\mid r,\\
 0,&p-1\nmid r.
 \end{cases} \tag{2}
\]
Indeed, the term \(x=0\) contributes zero, and the nonzero elements form a cyclic group of order \(p-1\). If \(g\) is a generator, the sum over the nonzero elements is
\[
 \sum_{j=0}^{p-2}g^{rj}.
\]
If \(g^r=1\), equivalently \(p-1\mid r\), every term is \(1\), so the sum is \(p-1=-1\) in \(\mathbb F_p\). Otherwise this is a geometric series with ratio different from \(1\), and hence its sum is zero.

Consequently,
\[
 p\mid\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}k^r
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p-1\nmid r. \tag{3}
\]

More generally, suppose \(p\mid n\), say \(n=pt\). Breaking the integers \(0,1,\ldots,n-1\) into \(t\) consecutive blocks of length \(p\), each block contains every residue modulo \(p\) once. Therefore
\[
 \sum_{k=0}^{n-1}k^r\equiv
 t\sum_{x\in\mathbb F_p}x^r\pmod p. \tag{4}
\]
In particular,
\[
 p\mid\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}k^r
\]
whenever either \(p\mid t=n/p\), or \(p-1\nmid r\). We shall repeatedly use this observation.

## 2. The required Bernoulli denominator theorem

For an odd prime \(p\), let \(v_p\) be the usual \(p\)-adic valuation on nonzero rational numbers. We need the following part of the von Staudt–Clausen theorem:

**Lemma.** Let \(p\ge3\) be prime and \(r\ge1\). Then:

1. \(v_p(B_i)\ge-1\) for every \(i\ge0\) (with the assertion automatic when \(B_i=0\));
2. if \(p-1\mid r\), then \(v_p(B_r)=-1\); equivalently,
   \[
   v_p(D_r)=1\quad\text{and}\quad p\nmid N_r;
   \tag{5}
   \]
3. if \(p-1\nmid r\), then \(p\nmid D_r\).

Here is a proof of exactly these assertions. Faulhaber’s formula, in the Bernoulli convention being used, is
\[
 \sum_{k=0}^{b-1}k^r
 =\sum_{i=0}^{r}B_i\binom{r+1}{i}\frac{b^{r+1-i}}{r+1}. \tag{6}
\]
The last term, corresponding to \(i=r\), is \(B_rb\). Thus
\[
 \sum_{k=0}^{b-1}k^r=T_r(b)+B_rb, \tag{7}
\]
where
\[
 T_r(b)=\sum_{i=0}^{r-1}B_i\binom{r+1}{i}\frac{b^{r+1-i}}{r+1}. \tag{8}
\]
For \(i\le r\), the elementary binomial identity
\[
 \binom{r+1}{i}(r+1-i)=(r+1)\binom ri
\]
gives
\[
 \binom{r+1}{i}\frac{b^{r+1-i}}{r+1}
 =\binom ri\frac{b^{r+1-i}}{r+1-i}. \tag{9}
\]
Hence, for a nonzero summand and \(j=r+1-i\), its valuation is
\[
 v_p(B_i)+v_p\!\binom ri+jv_p(b)-v_p(j). \tag{10}
\]

We first prove \(v_p(B_r)\ge-1\) by strong induction on \(r\); the initial value \(B_0=1\) is clear. Apply (7) with \(b=p\). For every term in the tail, \(i<r\), so \(j=r+1-i\ge1\). By induction \(v_p(B_i)\ge-1\), while the binomial coefficient has nonnegative valuation. Also
\[
 v_p(j)+1\le j. \tag{11}
\]
To see this, put \(e=v_p(j)\). Since \(p^e\mid j\), we have \(p^e\le j\), and \(e+1\le 2^e\le p^e\) for \(e\ge1\), while the case \(e=0\) is immediate. Formula (10), with \(b=p\), therefore shows that every tail term has valuation at least zero. A finite sum of such terms also has valuation at least zero, unless it is zero, which causes no difficulty. The power sum on the left of (7) is an integer, so it too is \(p\)-integral. It follows from
\[
 B_rp=\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}k^r-T_r(p)
\]
that \(v_p(B_rp)\ge0\), and hence \(v_p(B_r)\ge-1\). This completes the induction.

We can sharpen the estimate on the tail. For \(i<r\), we have \(j=r+1-i\ge2\). Since \(p\ge3\),
\[
 v_p(j)+2\le j. \tag{12}
\]
If \(v_p(j)=0\), this follows from \(j\ge2\). If \(e=v_p(j)\ge1\), then \(e+2\le3^e\le p^e\le j\). Combining (10), the already proved lower bound \(v_p(B_i)\ge-1\), and (12), we find
\[
 v_p(T_r(p))\ge1, \tag{13}
\]
unless the tail is zero, in which case the same divisibility assertion is still true.

If \(p-1\mid r\), equation (2) says that the integer power sum in (7) is congruent to \(-1\pmod p\), and hence has valuation zero. The tail has valuation at least one, so (7) forces
\[
 v_p(B_rp)=0,
\]
and therefore \(v_p(B_r)=-1\).

If \(p-1\nmid r\), equation (2) says that the power sum is divisible by \(p\). Both it and the tail in (7) have valuation at least one, so \(v_p(B_rp)\ge1\), whence \(v_p(B_r)\ge0\).

Finally, because \(N_r/D_r\) is reduced, a prime cannot divide both \(N_r\) and \(D_r\). Thus \(v_p(B_r)=-1\) means exactly that \(p\) occurs to exponent one in \(D_r\) and does not divide \(N_r\). Likewise, if \(v_p(B_r)\ge0\), then \(p\) cannot divide \(D_r\), for otherwise reducedness would give \(v_p(N_r)=0\) and hence a negative valuation. This proves the lemma.

## 3. A local congruence from Faulhaber’s formula

We next derive the key congruence relating the Bernoulli number to the power sum.

**Local congruence.** Let \(p\ge3\) be prime, let \(r\ge1\), suppose \(p\mid n\), and suppose \(p-1\mid r\). If \(B_r=N_r/D_r\) is reduced, then
\[
 D_r\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}k^r-N_rn\equiv0\pmod{p^2}. \tag{14}
\]

To prove it, use (7) with base \(b=n\):
\[
 \sum_{k=0}^{n-1}k^r=T_r(n)+B_rn.
\]
Multiplying by \(D_r\) gives the exact rational identity
\[
 D_r\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}k^r-N_rn=D_rT_r(n). \tag{15}
\]
The left side is an integer, so it remains to show that the right side has \(p\)-adic valuation at least two.

By (5), \(v_p(D_r)=1\). For each term in \(T_r(n)\), formula (10) applies with \(b=n\). Since \(p\mid n\), we have \(v_p(n)\ge1\). Also \(i<r\), so \(j=r+1-i\ge2\). Thus, using \(v_p(B_i)\ge-1\), nonnegativity of the valuation of the binomial coefficient, and (12),
\[
\begin{aligned}
 v_p\left(B_i\binom ri\frac{n^j}{j}\right)
 &\ge -1+j-v_p(j)\\
 &\ge1.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore \(v_p(T_r(n))\ge1\), unless the tail is zero. In either event (15) is divisible by \(p^2\), because \(D_r\) contributes one further factor of \(p\). This proves (14).

## 4. The main divisibility equivalence

We now prove
\[
 n^2\mid Nn+D
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 n\mid S+1, \tag{16}
\]
where, as at the beginning, \(m=n-1\), \(B_m=N/D\), and \(S=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}k^m\).

### The case \(n=2\)

Here \(m=1\) and \(B_1=-\tfrac12\), so \(N=-1\), \(D=2\), and
\[
 Nn+D=-2+2=0,
\]
which is divisible by \(n^2=4\). Also
\[
 S=0^1+1^1=1,
\]
so \(S+1=2\) is divisible by \(n=2\). Thus (16) holds.

### Even \(n\ge4\)

Now \(m=n-1\) is odd and greater than one. The odd Bernoulli numbers beyond \(B_1\) vanish, so \(B_m=0\), hence \(N=0\) and \(D=1\). Therefore \(Nn+D=1\), which is not divisible by \(n^2\).

We show that \(n\nmid S+1\) as well. Work modulo \(n\). Negation permutes all residue classes modulo \(n\), and because \(m\) is odd,
\[
 S=\sum_{x\bmod n}x^m
   =\sum_{x\bmod n}(-x)^m
   =-S\pmod n.
\]
Thus \(2S\equiv0\pmod n\). If \(S+1\equiv0\pmod n\), then multiplying by two gives \(2S+2\equiv0\pmod n\). Subtracting \(2S\equiv0\) would yield \(2\equiv0\pmod n\), impossible for \(n\ge4\). Hence both sides of (16) are false.

### Odd \(n\)

It remains to treat odd \(n\). By unique factorization, divisibility by \(n\) or \(n^2\) can be tested one prime at a time. Let \(p\mid n\) be prime and put
\[
 \alpha=v_p(n)\ge1.
\]
Because \(n\) is odd, \(p\ge3\). We prove the local equivalence
\[
 p^{2\alpha}\mid Nn+D
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 p^\alpha\mid S+1. \tag{17}
\]
There are three cases.

#### Case 1: \(p-1\nmid m\)

By the Bernoulli denominator lemma, \(p\nmid D\). Since \(p\mid n\), we have
\[
 Nn+D\equiv D\not\equiv0\pmod p.
\]
Thus the left side of (17) is false.

On the other hand, (4) and (2) show that \(p\mid S\), because \(p-1\nmid m\). Hence \(S+1\not\equiv0\pmod p\), so the right side of (17) is also false.

#### Case 2: \(p-1\mid m\) and \(\alpha\ge2\)

The Bernoulli denominator lemma gives
\[
 v_p(D)=1. \tag{18}
\]
Since \(p^2\mid n\), we have \(p^2\mid Nn\). If \(p^{2\alpha}\) divided \(Nn+D\), then in particular \(p^2\mid Nn+D\); subtracting \(Nn\) would imply \(p^2\mid D\), contradicting (18). Thus the left side of (17) is false.

For the right side, write \(n=pt\). Since \(\alpha\ge2\), \(p\mid t\). Formula (4) therefore gives \(S\equiv0\pmod p\), regardless of the value of the residue-class power sum. Thus \(S+1\not\equiv0\pmod p\), and the right side is false too.

#### Case 3: \(p-1\mid m\) and \(\alpha=1\)

The local congruence (14) gives
\[
 DS-Nn\equiv0\pmod{p^2}. \tag{19}
\]
Consequently,
\[
 D(S+1)=(Nn+D)+(DS-Nn),
\]
so (19) implies
\[
 p^2\mid Nn+D
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 p^2\mid D(S+1). \tag{20}
\]
Again \(v_p(D)=1\), so write
\[
 D=pD',\qquad p\nmid D'.
\]
Euclid’s lemma then gives
\[
 p^2\mid D(S+1)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 p\mid S+1. \tag{21}
\]
Since \(\alpha=1\), equations (20) and (21) are exactly (17).

This proves (17) for every prime divisor \(p\) of the odd integer \(n\). For a prime not dividing \(n\), the relevant exponent in both \(n\) and \(n^2\) is zero, so there is no condition. Unique factorization now yields (16).

Combining the cases \(n=2\), even \(n\ge4\), and odd \(n\), we have proved (16) for every \(n>1\).

## 5. Relating the divisibility to the sequence denominator

By definition,
\[
 a(n)=\operatorname{den}\left(\frac{N}{n}+\frac{D}{n^2}\right),
\]
where \(\operatorname{den}\) means the positive denominator after reducing the rational number. But
\[
 \frac{N}{n}+\frac{D}{n^2}=\frac{Nn+D}{n^2}. \tag{22}
\]
A rational number with integer numerator and positive integer denominator has reduced denominator \(1\) exactly when the displayed denominator divides the numerator. Therefore
\[
 a(n)=1
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 n^2\mid Nn+D. \tag{23}
\]
Combining (23) with (16), for every \(n>1\) we obtain the promised pointwise equivalence
\[
 a(n)=1
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 n\mid\left(\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}k^{n-1}+1\right). \tag{24}
\]
Because \(n>1\), the term \(k=0\) is zero, so this is the usual Agoh–Giuga condition
\[
 \sum_{k=1}^{n-1}k^{n-1}\equiv-1\pmod n.
\]

## 6. Equivalence of the conjectures

Assume first the A309132 conjecture: for every \(n>1\),
\[
 a(n)=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad n\text{ is prime}.
\]
Using (24), this becomes
\[
 n\mid\left(\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}k^{n-1}+1\right)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad n\text{ is prime},
\]
which is exactly the Agoh–Giuga conjecture.

Conversely, assume the Agoh–Giuga conjecture: for every \(n>1\), the displayed power-sum divisibility holds if and only if \(n\) is prime. Replacing that divisibility by the equivalent condition \(a(n)=1\) from (24) gives
\[
 a(n)=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad n\text{ is prime}
\]
for every \(n>1\), which is the A309132 conjecture.

Thus the conjecture that \(a(n)=1\) exactly for primes \(n>1\) is equivalent to the Agoh–Giuga conjecture.
